lessons.title: From Berry curvature to sheet Hall response
lessons.summary: Fix charge, coordinate, and Berry-connection conventions before converting quantum geometry into current response.

sections.title: Clarify which current responds to which field
sections.text: This site uses electron charge −e (e>0), Berry connection A=i〈u|∂u〉 and orientation from kx to ky. σxy denotes x current driven by y electric field. Under these definitions, filling a lower band with C=+1 gives negative σxy, consistent with references that instead call σyx the Hall conductance.

sections.title: Include occupations of both bands
sections.text: The two QWZ bands have energies ±s|d| and opposite Berry curvatures. When chemical potential enters the upper band, its newly occupied states partly cancel the lower-band curvature contribution. If both bands are empty or both full, the net curvature response of this complete two-band space vanishes.

sections.title: The difference between zero-temperature insulators and metals
sections.text: At zero temperature with chemical potential inside the direct gap, the lower band is full and the upper empty, leaving the lower-band Chern number in the integral. Entering a band or heating gives occupations that no longer fill a complete isolated band, so response is generally unquantized. A two-dimensional sheet response needs no arbitrary vacuum thickness.

sections.title: Symmetry determines which contributions can offset
sections.text: Time-reversal symmetry cancels paired curvature/occupation contributions and forbids intrinsic charge anomalous Hall response. Breaking it permits a possible response but does not allow arbitrary tensor components in every magnetic group; other crystal symmetries must also be checked.

lessons.title: Fermi entropy and transverse thermoelectric response
lessons.summary: The same curvature map, using occupancy and entropy as different weights, will produce different response curves.

sections.title: temperature gradient corresponds to transport thermoelectric coefficient
sections.text: Equilibrium magnetization circulating currents are not directly transport currents through the sample. After subtracting them, intrinsic transverse thermoelectric coefficients can be written as Brillouin-zone integrals of curvature weighted by Fermi entropy.

sections.title: There is no Fermi entropy in either the full state or the empty state
sections.text: s(f) is zero at f=0 and f=1, and is maximum at f=1/2. States in the range of about several kBT near the chemical potential are most sensitive to thermoelectric . The entropy-weighted curvature in the figure is not the electron density, nor can it have the same numerical meaning as the occupancy-weighted curvature.

sections.title: Why can α in the middle of the Hall platform be zero?
sections.text: The two bands of this model are symmetric about zero energy and have opposite curvatures. At μ=0, the entropy weights of the two bands are the same, and α_{xy} cancels out point by point; but the occupation difference can still be non-zero, and σxy can be very large. Changing the sign of μ, σxy maintains even symmetry while α_{xy} changes sign.

sections.title: Connection to Low Temperature Energy Derivatives
sections.text: When the continuum has converged and the zero-temperature Hall curve is sufficiently smooth within the thermal window, the thermoelectric response can be related to its energy derivative by Mott expansion. Directly differencing the step occupancy of coarse meshes can create spikes; this experiment uses an entropy kernel to integrate directly and compare the finer meshes independently. If SI system kB is used here, ε in the energy derivative must be measured in joules; the eV input in the interface must be converted first.
sections.formula: Under the agreement on this page: α_{xy}≈−[π²kB²T/(3e)] ∂σxy⁰/∂ε |μ

lessons.title: From response coefficients to credible experimental explanations
lessons.summary: Distinguish local curvature, integrated coefficients, and open-circuit signals, and include convergence checks in research conclusions.

sections.title: α_{xy} is not an open circuit Nernst voltage
sections.text: If the total current is required to be zero in the experiment, the electric field needs to offset the current generated by the temperature gradient. The response is now the inverse matrix of the full conductance tensor multiplied by the full thermoelectric tensor. Knowing only the intrinsic transverse components, the longitudinal scattering response cannot be automatically completed, nor should tensors from different models be spliced.

sections.title: Grid integer and curvature integral convergence are two different things
sections.text: The existing FHS lesson emphasizes discrete Chern integers, whereas this page directly integrates curvature. Every run compares N×N and 2N×2N meshes and checks the curvature integral against the analytical lower-band Chern number. Each μ-scan point has its own stability indicator; a passing selected point does not establish that every scan point passes.
sections.formula: I_Ω(N)=2π〈Ω_{−}〉N; compare I_Ω with analytic C and examine response changes on mesh refinement

sections.title: Stop using this page’s band-resolved formulas at analytical gap closure
sections.text: At m=−2,0,2, the analytical gap is zero even if an odd mesh misses the degenerate momentum. This implementation therefore stops reporting responses that require isolated bands. It does not declare every gapless material’s physical Hall effect undefined; this is a limitation of the current algorithm.

sections.title: From teaching model to material
sections.text: bcc Fe provides magnetic-metal context for learning about curvature hotspots near SOC-induced avoided crossings and integration convergence. These QWZ parameters are not fitted to Fe. Complete Wannier responses also need position/connection matrices, orbital embedding and conventions; one hr file is not automatically all the Berry information.
sections.formula: Model reproduction, source data, units and convergence records should be retained at the same time

lessons.title: From closed energy level to device connected to electrode
lessons.summary: Put finite chain, semi-infinite lead and conductance at both ends in the same model.

sections.title: device requires boundary conditions
sections.text: A closed finite chain has discrete eigenlevels. Transport additionally needs left and right electrodes as particle reservoirs. Here two identical semi-infinite uniform chains connect to the first and last sites of a finite scattering region, either uniform or an alternating-bond SSH chain. Hamiltonian off-diagonal hopping elements carry the minus sign −t.

sections.title: electrode only provides propagation channel within the band
sections.text: The uniform lead band spans ε₀±2t₀. Its retarded surface Green function must have nonpositive imaginary part and approach 1/E far from the band. Contact self-energies encode open boundaries in the finite matrix; contact hopping v is not an independent relaxation time.

sections.title: The difference between transmission probability and conductance
sections.text: Each spin electrode has at most one propagation channel, and the transmission T is between 0 and 1. The zero temperature linear conductance is g_s(e²/h)T(E_F). g_s=2 is just two identical and independent spin channels and cannot be used to replace the real spin–orbit coupling ; the energy slider on the page specifies E_F.

sections.title: The ideal chain is the first benchmark
sections.text: If scattering-region hoppings, onsite energies and contacts match the electrodes, there is no physical in-band reflection and T=1 as η→0. A positive numerical imaginary part gives small artificial absorption, shown together with conservation residuals. Group velocity vanishes exactly at a band edge, so that point is not treated as an open propagating channel.

lessons.title: Potential barrier, resonance and local spectrum
lessons.summary: Compare devices with spectral peaks that may nevertheless have different transmission.

sections.title: A station can also reflect electrons
sections.text: Adding an onsite potential V to a matched uniform chain produces finite reflection through interference of scattering amplitudes. For a single-site barrier with t=1 and all other onsite energies zero, analytical transmission independently checks the program. Moving that barrier does not change its transmission probability on an infinite uniform background.

sections.title: Weak contact turns discrete energy levels into resonance
sections.text: The transmission peak of a weak contact finite chain is usually located near the energy level shifted and broadened by the electrode. Symmetrical contacts give very high transmission at resonance but low T away from resonance. Increasing contact not only changes the width but also changes the energy level and interference. It cannot be inferred that T of a fixed energy must increase just because the contact is stronger.

sections.title: Local density of states is not transmission probability
sections.text: LDOS describes the local spectral weights at each site for the selected energy; the left and right injection densities further illustrate which spectral weights can be excited by the respective electrodes. When the contact on one side is set to 0, LDOS peaks can still appear, while the transmission at both ends is strictly 0. The LDOS in the figure is given per spin, per eV, not electron occupation number.

sections.title: scan needs to resolve narrow peaks
sections.text: The discrete points of a single energy scan do not prove that all resonances have been sampled. The scanning window should be narrowed, the sampling points should be increased, and eta should be changed at the same time; do not mistake a beautiful smooth curve for a converged result by artificially increasing eta.

lessons.title: SSH terminal states, contacts and flux continuity
lessons.summary: connects existing Zak phase and finite chain spectrum to a truly open two-terminal device.

sections.title: Keep the same intracell/intercell convention
sections.text: Bond 0 connects sites 0 and 1 and is the intracell bond t₁=t×dimerRatio; the next is the intercell bond t₂=t. An even-site chain with weak intracell bonds may have low-energy edge states. At finite length, the two endpoint wavefunctions overlap, so their energies generally are not exactly zero. An overall minus sign on hopping does not change the SSH Zak phase modulo 2π, but comparisons still require consistent orbital and cell conventions.
sections.formula: t₁=t×dimerRatio; t₂=t; an isolated N=12 chain can be compared with the periodic model at the same parameters

sections.title: Edge states do not guarantee high conductance
sections.text: In the same chain of N=12, t₁=.6, t₂=1, at E=.05 eV, changing the contact from .15 to .8 eV changes the resonance width and coupling; T needs to be calculated instead of just observing the endpoint LDOS. This course uses presets to keep the model and energy the same and only change the contacts.
sections.formula: Geometry/Topology Diagnosis → Closed Chain Energy Level → Electrode Self-Energy → T(E)

sections.title: Check the current on every bond
sections.text: Take the unit incident flux of the left electrode, ψ=√Γ_LGʳe₁, and the forward bond flux is defined as flowing from site i to i+1. In the absence of real scattering or absorption, the fluxes of each bond are the same; the losses introduced by the value eta can be accurately calculated at each site. This dimensionless flux is not a finite bias ampere current.

sections.title: Bringing computational evidence back to the research record
sections.text: Save T(E), selected energy, LDOS, eta comparison and continuity residuals under two contacts, and then write whether the conclusion is supported. The Zak phase cannot be deduced only from the transmission peaks at both ends; the real material still requires complete orbit, electrode, scattering and structural parameters.

lessons.title: From ten single-electron states to fixed-N Fock space
lessons.summary: The many-electron dimension follows fermionic occupations; the number of single-electron levels is not the number of many-electron states.

sections.title: Each spin orbital can be occupied only once
sections.text: Use the five real d orbitals xy,yz,xz,x²−y²,3z²−r², each with up and down spin. At fixed N, select N of the ten spin orbitals to form antisymmetric Slater determinants. Program bitstrings record these occupations, and exchange signs follow from fermionic anticommutation. N=6 gives 210 determinants, not ten single-electron levels multiplied by six.

sections.title: Resolve conserved quantities before computing energy levels
sections.text: This model has no SOC, magnetic field, or spin-dependent  crystal field . Total electron number and Sz are conserved, allowing blocks labeled by N↑ and N↓. The complete Hund spin-flip term preserves total spin SU(2). Diagonalize H within each block, then S² within equal-energy subspaces to avoid arbitrary numerical mixing at accidental degeneracies.

sections.title: Read multielectron energy levels and occupations correctly
sections.text: The table groups states with equal energy and S, including 2S+1 magnetic components and possible orbital multiplicity in the degeneracy. Orbital occupations lie between 0 and 2 and sum to N over five orbitals. Trace averages over a joint degenerate subspace do not depend on the eigensolver's basis choice. Complete atomic LS term symbols are not provided here.

lessons.title: Why Hund exchange requires spin flips and pair hopping
lessons.summary: Verify interactions from the analytic two-electron limit rather than relying only on the rule to make spins as parallel as possible.

sections.title: Three density-repulsion terms and two exchange processes
sections.text: Opposite-spin electrons in the same orbital cost U. Opposite-spin density terms in different orbitals cost U−2J; same-spin terms cost U−3J. Additionally, −J S⁺_mS⁻_n exchanges spins between orbitals, while +J P†_mP_n transfers a pair to another orbital. With these terms retained, eigenstates cannot all be identified with fixed occupation diagrams.

sections.title: The zero-crystal-field d² case can be solved by hand
sections.text: For two electrons in five degenerate orbitals, spin triplets have antisymmetric orbital pairs, energy U−3J, and dimension 3×C(5,2)=30. Of the remaining 15 spin singlets, 14 have energy U−J and one fully symmetric doubly occupied combination has U+4J. For J>0 the triplets are lowest; the program checks signs and multiplicities against this full analytic spectrum.

sections.title: Why changing U at fixed N does not change the spin
sections.text: Adding the U coefficients of the three density terms gives exactly the number N(N−1)/2 of occupied spin-orbital pairs. Increasing U therefore shifts the entire fixed-N spectrum and cannot by itself drive a high-/low-spin change in this isolated model. J and crystal-field splitting alter relative energies; charge fluctuations, ligands and bandwidth in real materials require a larger model.

lessons.title: Crystal field versus Hund coupling: from d⁶ spin crossover to the limits of the NiO analogy
lessons.summary: Compare weak- and strong-field many-electron ground states to understand occupation mixing, crossings, and model validity.

sections.title: Two limits of d⁶
sections.text: In an octahedral field, three t₂g orbitals are lower and two e_g orbitals higher. Hund exchange favors larger spin at weak field: the Δ=0.5 eV, J=0.6 eV preset has S=2. At the same N,U,J, the strong-field Δ=6 eV preset has S=0. Pair hopping causes occupations to deviate slightly from a closed t₂g⁶ shell, so use the computed expectation values.

sections.title: Trial occupation diagrams explain trends, not exact critical points
sections.text: The high-spin d⁶ trial determinant has t₂g⁴e_g² and crystal-field energy −0.4Δ; the low-spin t₂g⁶ trial state has energy −2.4Δ. The latter gains 2Δ in crystal-field energy but loses its Hund-exchange advantage. Full pair hopping mixes double-occupancy configurations, so ground states must be compared after diagonalization. Neighboring points on a plotted scan do not determine an exact crossing.
sections.formula: E_CF(t₂g⁶)−E_CF(t₂g⁴e_g²)=−2Δ; the crossover is determined by the full many-electron spectrum

sections.title: NiO supplies physical context, not automatically fitted parameters
sections.text: Local Ni²⁺ in NiO is usually discussed in a d⁸ coordination setting. Multielectron crystal fields require Coulomb exchange, not just a single-electron splitting diagram. Here a simplified Kanamori model with one common J and original teaching parameters is used; the full d-shell Slater interaction has independent angular structure, while ligand hybridization and charge transfer enlarge the space further. The present levels are not presented as a fitted NiO excitation spectrum.
sections.formula: Kanamori(U,J) ≠ complete Slater(F⁰,F²,F⁴) ≠ a ligand charge-transfer model

exercises.title: is pushed from the curvature integral to the Hall platform
exercises.prompt: fixed electron charge −e, A=i〈u|∂u〉, xy orientation; lower band C=+1, upper band C=−1.

steps.prompt: At zero temperature and μ is within the energy gap, what are the occupations of the two bands?
steps.hint: lower band are lower than μ.
choices: The lower band is full and the upper band is empty
steps.explanation: The complete occupation of the isolated lower band is the prerequisite for using single-band Chern to give a quantization platform.

steps.prompt: Under the definition of j_x=σxyEy on this page, what is σxy?
steps.hint: There is a negative sign brought by the electron charge before the formula.
steps.explanation: σxy=−C e²/h; σyx=+e²/h of the same system.

steps.prompt: What do you get when you raise μ above two bands?
steps.hint: The curvature sum of the complete two-band space is zero point by point.
choices: Contributions of two fully occupied bands cancel
steps.explanation: Upper/lower curvatures are opposite and occupations equal, so the net intrinsic Hall term vanishes.

steps.prompt: What are the two-dimensional σxy units output by this model?
steps.hint: No material thickness specified.
choices: S/m, using any vacuum layer thickness
steps.explanation: The two-dimensional current is calculated per width, and the sheet conductance unit is S; three-dimensional conversion requires physical thickness.

exercises.title: Use entropy weight to determine horizontal direction thermoelectric
exercises.prompt: Using the ±E two bands and opposite curvatures of QWZ, infer the effects of μ and temperature.

steps.prompt: Which occupation has the largest dimensionless Fermi entropy?
steps.hint: Compares completely certain versus least certain binary occupancies.
steps.explanation: s(1/2)=ln2; the entropy of both the full state and the empty state is 0.

steps.prompt: μ=0, the entropy of the two symmetric energy bands is equal, what about α_{xy}?
steps.hint: The two bands have opposite curvatures.
choices: is equal to the Chern number
steps.explanation: has equal entropy kernels but opposite curvatures. It cannot be concluded that α_{xy} is non-zero based on σxy being non-zero.

steps.prompt: What does this model have to do with just changing μ from a positive value to the opposite negative value?
steps.hint: Particle–hole symmetry exchanges the two bands’ thermal windows.
choices: σxy is unchanged; α_{xy} changes sign
σxy changes sign; α_{xy} is unchanged
steps.explanation: σ is the even function of μ, and α is the odd function of μ, which can be used as a calculation check.

steps.prompt: T=0, how should the thermoelectric coefficient be handled?
steps.hint: There is no longer an entropy window of finite width at strictly zero temperature.
choices: is given an arbitrary value by the coarse difference of the stepped σ curve
is forced to equal the quantized Hall conductance
steps.explanation: Metal low temperature α usually goes to zero with T; this implementation explicitly uses α_{xy}(T=0)=0.

exercises.title: Write a verifiable conclusion for lateral response
exercises.prompt: A set of coarse mesh curvature integrals gives nice looking values to determine what information is missing.

steps.prompt: At m=−2 an odd mesh misses the gap-closing point. Can a gapped plateau be claimed?
steps.hint: The analytical gap is independent of the display mesh.
choices: As long as all samples have gaps, it can
As long as the result is close to an integer
No; analytical gap closure leaves the main response blank
steps.explanation: The algorithm first uses the analytic gap to prevent missed degeneracy points.

steps.prompt: The N and 2N results of selected μ are close to each other. Can this prove that the entire μ scan has converged?
steps.hint: The thermal window moves with the chemical potential.
choices: No, each scanning point must be checked separately.
Yes, all parameters share one convergence
As long as the grid is an odd number
steps.explanation: page retains independent stable markers for each scan point.

steps.prompt: only gives α_{xy}, can it be read directly as the open circuit Nernst voltage?
steps.hint: An open circuit must satisfy that the entire current vector is zero.
choices: Yes, both units are the same
No, the complete σ and α tensors of the same system are needed.
steps.explanation: open circuit thermoelectric tensor is S=σ⁻¹α; the unit A/K of α_{xy} is also different from the voltage thermoelectric coefficient.

steps.prompt: If the QWZ parameter is named Fe, is it equivalent to calculating the response of real iron?
steps.hint: The model parameters are from different sources than the material matrix elements.
choices: Yes, the name determines the material
Yes, as long as the curve shape is similar
No, independent material data, convention and convergence verification required
steps.explanation: bcc Fe provides physics background here; current calculations remain an explicit two-band teaching model.

exercises.title: From one propagation channel to the conductance at both ends
exercises.prompt: Considering t₀=t=1 eV, ε₀=0, uniform chains with fully matched contacts, first take eta → 0.

steps.prompt: In what energy range does the electrode have propagated states?
steps.hint: is judged by E=ε₀−2t₀cos k.
steps.explanation: The cosine range is −1 to 1; the band edge group velocity is zero and cannot be regarded as a normal open channel point.

steps.prompt: E=.2 eV, what is the ideal transmission when there is no barrier?
steps.hint: The scattering region is a segment of an infinite uniform chain.
choices: depends on the number of sites, must be 1/N
steps.explanation: A perfectly matched chain has no reflections; one channel per spin is fully transmitted when eta → 0.

steps.prompt: If there is only one spin copy, what is the conductance at this time?
steps.hint: Do not apply the commonly used 2e²/h unconditionally.
steps.explanation: g_s=1, G=(e²/h)T=e²/h; it is conductance, not resistance.

steps.prompt: is changed to two independent copies of the same spin. Which one changes?
steps.hint: Hamiltonian and per-spin scattering processes remain the same.
choices: The total conductance doubles, T per spin remains unchanged
steps.explanation: g_s=2 only adds the conductances of the same independent channels; no SOC or spin flips are introduced.

exercises.title: Hand-calculated single-point potential barrier and disconnection electrode
exercises.prompt: Take t=1 eV and E=0, then add one onsite potential V=2 eV to a matched quantum wire.

steps.prompt: What is T obtained from the analytical formula?
steps.hint: Substitute into (4t²−E²)/(4t²−E²+V²).
steps.explanation: is 4 and the denominator is 4+4=8, so T=1/2.

steps.prompt: What is the reflection R when η→0?
steps.hint: single-channel elastic scattering meets T+R=1.
steps.explanation: R=1−T=1/2; the sum of the probabilities cannot exceed 1.

steps.prompt: To set the right contact to 0 but still retain the finite chain, which item must be 0?
steps.hint: T contains Γ_LΓ_R, while LDOS is still from the finite chain spectrum.
steps.explanation: zero right contact means Γ_R=0, T=0; having local spectral weight does not mean cross-device transmission.

steps.prompt: The two scan curves seem to have no narrow peaks. What is the most reliable way to check?
steps.hint: distinguishes between energy resolution and artificial broadening.
choices: Only increase η to make the graph smoother
Narrow the scan window, refine sampling and compare smaller η
steps.explanation: Check energy-grid refinement separately from η convergence; coarse grids can miss weak-contact resonances.

exercises.title: From terminal state to inspectable device conclusion
exercises.prompt: For the same SSH finite chain, only the contact strength is changed, and the finite positive number η is used for calculation.

steps.prompt: The endpoint LDOS is very large. Can we directly declare that the conductance at both ends is very large?
steps.hint: where one side of the contact is disconnected may still have local spectral peaks.
choices: No, it also depends on the coupling and propagation on both sides
Yes, as long as the number of endpoints is 2
steps.explanation: LDOS is the local spectral quantity, and T is the scattering quantity connecting the left and right electrodes.

steps.prompt: If T=.7, R=.29, A_η=.01, does the conservation pass?
steps.hint: Artificial losses cannot be omitted from the conservation equation.
choices: passes because the sum of the three is 1
steps.explanation: Limited η can cause reported artifactual absorption; T+R+A_η=1 should be verified and converge to η → 0.

steps.prompt: What is the correct continuity check for internal site i?
steps.hint: The loss is positive and the inflow is greater than the outflow.
steps.explanation: The positive imaginary regulator in the retarded calculation introduces a probability sink. With forward flux defined consistently, inflow minus outflow equals loss.

steps.prompt: After a weak-strong contact, what information should be retained to support the conclusion?
steps.hint: The calculation cannot be reproduced by just taking a peak graph.
choices: Just write the three words SSH
model, termination method, contact, energy, eta and sampling, as well as T/LDOS and residuals
steps.explanation: To distinguish material models, boundary conditions and numerical settings, and connect existing Zak/finite chain evidence, the topology cannot be determined from one transmission peak alone.

exercises.title: Count the d⁶ space and determine U's role
exercises.prompt: Five d orbitals, each with two spin states. Fix six electrons, omit SOC, and compare U with U+0.2 eV.

steps.prompt: How many single-electron spin orbitals are there?
steps.hint: Multiply the number of orbitals by the number of spin states per orbital.
steps.explanation: 5×2=10; fermionic occupations are selected among these ten spin orbitals.

steps.prompt: What is the many-electron space dimension at fixed N=6?
steps.hint: The same spin orbital cannot be occupied twice; electron labels are indistinguishable.
steps.explanation: Distinct occupation sets give independent Slater determinants: 210 in total.

steps.prompt: If U increases by 0.2 eV, how much do all d⁶ levels shift together?
steps.hint: Six electrons form 6×5/2 pairs.
steps.explanation: ΔE=0.2×15=3 eV; this is a common shift.

steps.prompt: Can changing only U switch the ground state from S=2 to S=0 here?
steps.hint: Compare energy differences within the same N sector.
choices: It depends only on the number of grid points
steps.explanation: All fixed-N states receive the same shift, leaving relative energies and eigenstates unchanged.

exercises.title: Derive d² Hund-multiplet energies and dimensions by hand
exercises.prompt: Take five degenerate orbitals, N=2, U=4 eV, and J=0.6 eV, retaining complete spin-flip and pair-hopping terms.

steps.prompt: What is the spin-triplet energy U−3J?
steps.explanation: The triplet energy is 2.2 eV; J>0 lowers it below both types of singlet.

steps.prompt: A triplet has C(5,2) antisymmetric orbital pairs. How many states does this give in total?
steps.hint: Each S=1 multiplet has 2S+1=3 magnetic components.

steps.prompt: Fourteen singlets have energy U−J and the fully symmetric doubly occupied singlet has U+4J. What are these energies?
steps.hint: Multiply the same J by −1 and +4, respectively.
steps.explanation: These singlet energies are 3.4 and 6.4 eV; pair hopping determines the splitting of double-occupancy combinations.

steps.prompt: Which independent count should agree with 30+14+1=45?
steps.hint: Choose two of ten spin orbitals.
steps.explanation: The complete fixed-N=2 space has dimension 45, and level multiplicities must cover the whole space.

exercises.title: Infer trends in spin competition from crystal-field occupations
exercises.prompt: Compare high-spin trial occupation t₂g⁴e_g² and low-spin trial occupation t₂g⁶ for octahedral d⁶; Δ>0, with zero orbital barycenter.

steps.prompt: What is the crystal-field energy of the high-spin trial state?
steps.explanation: The crystal-field contribution is −1.6Δ+1.2Δ=−0.4Δ.

steps.prompt: How much  crystal field  energy does the low-spin trial state gain relative to the high-spin trial state?
steps.explanation: The energy difference is −2Δ, so a larger crystal field favors paired occupancy of lower orbitals.

steps.prompt: For calculated S=2 and S=0, what are the corresponding S² values?
steps.hint: S² has eigenvalue S(S+1), in units of ℏ².
steps.explanation: S=2 gives 6 and S=0 gives 0; the value of S² must not be identified directly with S.

steps.prompt: Can the crossing of two trial occupation diagrams be treated as the exact critical Δ of the full model?
steps.hint: Pair hopping mixes configurations; a finite scan is also not continuous root finding.
choices: Yes; every occupation state is an eigenstate
Yes, provided U is large enough
No; compare the complete spectrum and refine the scan near the crossing
steps.explanation: The full interaction must be diagonalized. This model also omits self-consistent ligand, temperature and structural changes in real materials.

cases.title: QWZ: from quantum geometry to a Hall plateau
cases.summary: Compares lower-band Chern, full-band curvature integral, and zero-temperature sheet Hall responses under the same sign convention.
cases.kind: An analytically tractable two-dimensional teaching model
cases.assumption: A single two-band QWZ model does not contain spin degeneracy multiples; its boundary spectrum is not directly regarded as the device conductance of the connected electrode.

cases.title: bcc Fe context: SOC curvature hotspots and transverse response
cases.summary: Use the public bcc Fe tutorial to explain full-BZ integration for anomalous Hall response in magnetic metals, then demonstrate the integration mechanism with partial occupations in QWZ.
cases.kind: Real Materials Methods Background + QWZ Demonstration
cases.assumption: No Fe Wannier matrix elements are imported or fitted. All interactive values come from QWZ and must not be labeled as predictions or experimental data for iron.

cases.title: Critical Hotspot: Seemingly Stable Numbers and Real Applicability
cases.summary: Compare the coarse grid, refined grid and analytical closed gap near the critical area, and write the convergence range in the report.
cases.assumption: Finite-mesh comparisons are diagnostics only. This band-resolved algorithm stops at gap closure; that does not imply every gapless material lacks physical transverse response.

cases.title: Ideal quantum wire: from energy band channel to conductance quantum
cases.summary: Check T≈1 with a perfectly matched finite chain, add a potential barrier, and check with the analytical scattering formula.
cases.assumption: 1D non-interacting chain, identical electrodes, and linear response at zero temperature; does not fit specific metals or nanowires.
links: Periodic Tight Binding and Finite Systems

cases.title: Same SSH chain: Zak, end state and contact transmission
cases.summary: follows the conventions of t₁=.6 and t₂=1, moves from the periodic model to the N=12 finite chain, and then compares the weak and strong electrode contacts.
cases.assumption: Finite length splits end states; transmission at both ends depends on contact and energy. No real polyacetylene devices have been calculated, nor is the topology uniquely determined by a single peak.

cases.title: Weak contact resonance: the relationship between spectral peaks and transmission peaks
cases.summary: Compare the low-energy resonance of odd-numbered uniform chains and the counterexample of disconnecting the right electrode, examining energy sampling and numerical broadening.
cases.kind: Numerical methods and device boundary cases
cases.assumption: The contact electrode is an ideal semi-infinite single-channel chain; eta is just a numerical adjustment quantity, and the model has no actual inelastic scattering, finite bias, or electron interaction.

cases.title: Ideal d⁶ ion: from orbital splitting to high- and low-spin states
cases.summary: Keep electron number and interactions fixed, vary only the  crystal field  splitting, and compare ground-state spin, occupations, and the lowest excitation gap.
cases.assumption: No real compound or fitted parameters are specified. SOC, magnetic field, ligand hybridization, and temperature are excluded; a local spin crossover does not determine a real material's transition temperature.

cases.title: NiO context: what does a single-electron diagram omit?
cases.summary: Starting from the NiO coordination and orbital illustration, inspect exchange and many-electron occupations in the fixed d⁸ sector and the S=1 context.
cases.assumption: The site uses a Kanamori model with a common J, not complete Slater multiplets, a ligand charge-transfer model, or an experimental NiO spectrum. Preset energies are illustrative only.

cases.title: Analytic d² audit: verify the model by counting 45 dimensions
cases.summary: Use the complete analytic 30+14+1 spectrum to check Hund exchange, pair hopping, and degeneracy counting, then vary U to identify a common energy shift.
cases.kind: A many-electron benchmark solvable by hand
cases.assumption: Zero crystal field, five degenerate orbitals and a single positive Hund parameter. The listed multiplets belong to the Kanamori approximation; full atomic LS term symbols are not assigned.
